results.result: The authors developed genetic tools for Capsaspora owczarzaki, including methods for stable transgene expression using antibiotic resistance markers and gene targeting by homologous recombination, successfully generating a homozygous coYki deletion mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are well-supported by experimental data including successful generation of stable cell lines with multiple antibiotic markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), PCR-based genotyping (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E), sequencing confirmation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and qPCR showing loss of coYki expression (Figure 1J). The methodology is thoroughly documented and reproducible.

results.result: coYki is dispensable for cell proliferation in Capsaspora owczarzaki across multiple culture conditions (adherent, shaking, and within aggregates).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C43-C44, C47, C50, and C61 are consistently supported by proliferation assays showing no significant differences between WT and coYki-/- cells in adherent culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), shaking culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and EdU incorporation within aggregates (Figure 2A-B). This contrasts with the known role of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie in animal cell proliferation.

results.result: coYki regulates the three-dimensional shape of multicellular aggregates in Capsaspora, with coYki-/- aggregates showing significantly reduced circularity and curvature compared to WT aggregates, without affecting aggregate size.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C52-C57, and C60 are well-supported by quantitative morphological analysis showing coYki-/- aggregates are significantly less circular (Figure 2F, p<0.001), have reduced curvature (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and are flatter in 3D (Figure 2G), while aggregate size remains unchanged (Figure 2E). Time-lapse microscopy (Video 1) confirms dynamic morphological differences.

results.result: coYki regulates cytoskeletal dynamics at the cell cortex, with coYki-/- cells displaying excessive membrane blebbing (3.1 protrusions/minute), aberrant F-actin distribution, and less circular cortical shape.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C72-C76, C80-C87, and C111 are strongly supported by time-lapse microscopy showing increased protrusions in coYki-/- cells (Figure 4A, Video 2), LifeAct-mScarlet imaging demonstrating actin-depleted blebs (Figure 4C, Video 6), and rescue by coYki transgene expression (Figure 4A, Video 3). The phenotype is observed in both adherent cells and aggregates (Video 7).

results.result: The cytoskeletal abnormalities of individual coYki-/- cells causally underlie the abnormal 3D shape of coYki-/- aggregates, as demonstrated by blebbistatin rescue of both cellular blebbing and aggregate morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C88-C92 are strongly supported by blebbistatin experiments showing rescue of both membrane blebbing in individual cells (Figure 4D, Video 8) and aggregate circularity (Figure 4E-F). This pharmacological rescue provides compelling evidence for a causal link between cellular cytoskeletal defects and aggregate morphology.

results.result: coYki negatively regulates cell-substrate adhesion but does not affect cell-cell adhesion, with coYki-/- cells showing significantly increased substrate attachment after agitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 and C117 are supported by adhesion assays showing significantly more coYki-/- cells remain attached to substrate after agitation (Figure 3F, p<0.0001), more coYki-/- aggregates are substrate-adherent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), while cell-cell adhesion measured by cluster size is unchanged (Figure 3E). Mixed aggregate experiments (Figure 3A-D) confirm individual coYki-/- cells integrate normally.

results.result: HXRXXS phosphorylation motifs regulate coYki subcellular localization, with wild-type coYki showing cytoplasmic enrichment while the 4SA mutant shows nuclear accumulation, suggesting conserved phosphorylation-dependent regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 are supported by fluorescence microscopy showing mScarlet-coYki is cytoplasmic (Figure 5B, E, G) while mScarlet-coYki 4SA is nuclear/uniform (Figure 5C, F, H), with quantitative line traces confirming significant differences (Figure 5G-H, p<0.05). This demonstrates conservation of phosphorylation-dependent localization control.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis reveals 1205 differentially expressed genes in coYki-/- cells, with enrichment of actin-binding proteins and cell movement/migration categories, but notably no enrichment in cell proliferation or cell cycle categories.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104, C106, C109-C110 are supported by RNA-seq data showing 397 downregulated and 808 upregulated genes, enrichment of actin-binding proteins (Supplementary file 3), and IPA analysis showing cell movement/migration as top enriched categories (Figure 6C) with no enrichment in proliferation/cell cycle categories. This transcriptomic profile is consistent with the observed phenotypes.

results.result: The Hippo pathway has an ancestral role in cytoskeletal dynamics and multicellular morphogenesis predating animal multicellularity, which was co-opted during evolution to regulate cell proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C113-C114 represent the main evolutionary conclusion supported by the functional characterization showing coYki regulates cytoskeleton and morphology but not proliferation in Capsaspora (a pre-metazoan organism), contrasting with YAP/TAZ/Yorkie's proliferation role in animals. The phylogenetic position of Capsaspora (Figure 1B) and functional data collectively support this evolutionary inference, though the co-option claim (C114) involves some speculation.

results.result: The function of coYki as a transcriptional regulator and Hippo pathway effector is conserved between Capsaspora and animals, based on phosphorylation-dependent localization and previous heterologous expression studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 is supported by the current study's demonstration of phosphorylation-dependent localization (C99-C100) combined with cited prior work showing coYki can activate Hippo target genes in Drosophila (C32) and that Capsaspora Hippo kinase can phosphorylate coYki (C33). The integration of current and prior data supports conservation of transcriptional regulatory function.

results.result: The regulation of 3D tissue architecture is an ancient and conserved function of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie predating animal multicellularity, as suggested by phenotypic similarity between coYki-/- Capsaspora aggregates and YAP-/- medaka fish embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 draw parallels between the flattening phenotype in coYki-/- aggregates and YAP-/- medaka fish (Figure 6D, citing Porazinski et al., 2015). While the phenotypic similarity is noted, the authors acknowledge they "cannot rule out independent acquisition" of this function. The inference of ancient conservation requires additional comparative functional studies in other organisms.

results.result: Individual coYki-/- cells integrate normally into mixed aggregates without cell sorting, indicating the aberrant aggregate morphology is an emergent property requiring many coYki-/- cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by mixed aggregate experiments showing mCherry-labeled coYki-/- cells distribute similarly to WT cells without sorting (Figure 3A-D). This demonstrates individual coYki-/- cells can adhere and integrate normally, supporting the inference that abnormal morphology emerges from collective behavior of many mutant cells.

results.result: Calcium-dependent cell adhesion mediates aggregate integrity in Capsaspora, as demonstrated by rapid aggregate dissociation upon EGTA treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by experimental data showing EGTA treatment causes rapid aggregate dissociation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is blocked by excess calcium. This demonstrates calcium-dependent adhesion maintains aggregate integrity, though the specific adhesion molecules involved are not identified.

results.result: Contact-mediated inhibition of proliferation is absent in Capsaspora, as evidenced by homogeneous distribution of proliferating cells within aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49, C51 are supported by EdU labeling showing uniform distribution of proliferating cells throughout aggregates (Figure 2A), contrasting with mammalian cell clones that show increased proliferation at boundaries. This inference is reasonable given the data, though it is based on spatial distribution rather than direct mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Capsaspora undergoes F-actin-mediated amoeboid locomotion with actin-rich structures mediating cell-substrate interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by LifeAct-mScarlet imaging showing F-actin enrichment at the leading edge of moving cells and stationary foci on the basal surface (Figure 4B, Video 4). These observations support the inference of amoeboid locomotion and substrate adhesion structures, though detailed characterization of these structures is not provided.

results.result: Increased cell-substrate adhesion in coYki-/- cells may involve upregulation of integrin genes and/or altered cytoskeletal contractility affecting focal adhesion strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 are supported by RNA-seq showing upregulation of two integrin-β genes in coYki-/- cells (C120), cited literature on cytoskeletal regulation of focal adhesions (C122), and blebbistatin rescue of aggregate morphology (C124). However, the relative contributions of integrin upregulation versus altered contractility are not experimentally distinguished.

results.result: Time-lapse microscopy reveals distinct aggregate dynamics: WT aggregates are round, fuse but never undergo fission, while coYki-/- aggregates are dynamically asymmetrical and sometimes undergo fission.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by 6-day time-lapse microscopy (Video 1) showing these distinct behaviors. The observations are descriptive and well-documented, though the molecular mechanisms underlying aggregate fusion versus fission are not explored.

results.result: Cell-cell adhesion is similar between WT and coYki-/- cells, as measured by cluster size after gentle rotation in suspension.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by quantitative analysis showing similar numbers of cells per cluster for WT and coYki-/- cells after rotation (Figure 3E). This assay provides evidence for normal cell-cell adhesion, though it measures only initial adhesion formation rather than adhesion strength or dynamics.

results.result: F-actin is enriched at a circular cell cortex in WT cells with transient bursts of small F-actin puncta.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by LifeAct-mScarlet imaging at mid-height of WT cells (Figure 4B, Video 5) showing cortical F-actin enrichment and puncta. This descriptive observation characterizes normal cortical organization in Capsaspora.

results.result: coYki may regulate cytoskeletal dynamics through transcription-independent mechanisms, as reported in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is explicitly stated as speculation that cannot be formally excluded. While cited work in Drosophila (Xu et al., 2018) demonstrates transcription-independent regulation, no experiments in the current study directly test whether coYki's cytoskeletal effects are transcription-dependent or independent.

results.result: Cell migration and motility are enriched functional categories among YAP/TAZ target genes in mammalian systems, consistent with findings in Capsaspora.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 cite previous studies (Stein et al., 2015; Paczkowska et al., 2020) showing enrichment of migration/motility categories in mammalian YAP/TAZ target genes. These citations support the comparison with Capsaspora findings, though the authors are reporting prior work rather than generating new data.

results.result: The co-option of YAP/TAZ/Yorkie for cell proliferation control likely occurred early in the animal lineage and may have provided a mechanism coupling proliferation with cytoskeletal and mechanical properties.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 cites evidence that Hippo pathway activity is enriched in proliferating tissues in early-diverging animals (Coste et al., 2016), supporting early co-option. However, C116 is explicitly speculative about the evolutionary advantage of this coupling. The timing and selective advantage of co-option remain hypothetical without functional studies in additional organisms.

results.result: Round aggregate shape may provide selective advantages through predation avoidance, sedimentation rate optimization, or stress protection of interior cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 present evolutionary hypotheses about selective pressures favoring round aggregates. C125 cites prior work (Stanley, 1973) on predation-driven multicellularity, while C126-C128 are logical inferences about geometric and physical consequences. However, these remain untested hypotheses without experimental evidence for selective advantages in Capsaspora.

results.result: YAP/TAZ/Yorkie may have first evolved to regulate 3D shape of multicellular aggregates in unicellular ancestors, later acquiring organ size control functions in animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 are explicitly presented as speculation about evolutionary trajectory. While the functional data in Capsaspora support an ancestral role in morphology, the proposed evolutionary sequence and timing of function acquisition require comparative functional studies across multiple lineages and remain hypothetical.

results.result: Background information on developmental signaling pathways, the Hippo pathway in animals, and genomic conservation in unicellular relatives of animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C22, C29-C31, C93-C94 represent established knowledge and cited prior work providing context for the study. These are well-supported by appropriate citations and represent accurate summaries of the field, though they are not novel findings of this manuscript.

results.result: Capsaspora owczarzaki is a tractable model organism with aggregative multicellularity and genomic conservation of developmental regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C28, C35-C39, C118-C119 describe Capsaspora characteristics based on established knowledge and cited prior work. These claims accurately characterize the organism and justify its use as a model system, though they represent background rather than novel findings.
